title: AI Will Save Us from Oral Exams
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey closes a long series of posts against oral exams by arguing that the problem was never talking but judging. He distinguishes oral engagement as a learning activity, which he defends, from oral exams as a measurement instrument, which he says are invalid because of evaluator bias, power dynamics and performance anxiety. In his view oral exams have always been reaching for emergent thought, the moment a student synthesises something new, yet the assessment context makes that unlikely and evaluators cannot reliably capture it. He then proposes AI as a witness rather than a judge: transcription and analysis can surface patterns in student discourse with no grades attached. For those not ready for that, he suggests students record and annotate their own thinking to build metacognitive awareness. The piece is clearly an opinion built on earlier posts, and the AI proposal is a speculative alternative rather than an evidenced finding.
points: The author separates oral practice as a pedagogy, which he defends, from oral exams as a measurement tool, which he says confuses talk-as-learning with talk-as-assessment.
Oral exams are described as reaching for emergent thought, yet the evaluative frame, power dynamics and anxiety work against that.
He proposes AI as witness rather than grader, capturing discourse and revealing patterns without grades or the observer effect.
Collective discussion can be analysed to show how knowledge grows or is suppressed when students build on each other rather than perform for an examiner.
A low-tech alternative is self-recorded talk annotated by the student, which develops metacognitive awareness with no external evaluator.
quotes: Oral engagement as a learning activity is pedagogically defensible. Oral exams as a measurement instrument are not.
We’ve confused the value of talk-as-learning with the validity of talk-as-assessment and that confusion has allowed a fundamentally flawed practice to persist because it feels rigorous.
The problem is that the context of assessment makes it unlikely that true emergence will occur.
We’re looking for the right thing—emergent thought, genuine understanding-in-formation—but we’re looking for it in the wrong way, under the wrong conditions, with the wrong tools.
Transcription plus prompted analysis via AI is an ideal use case for orality. Not AI-as-grader. AI-as-witness.
This isn’t AI replacing human judgment in evaluation. This is AI revealing patterns in oral discourse that could inform learning, not gate-keeping.
This preserves the potential value of oral practice while removing the problematic evaluator relationship. It makes space for emergence while keeping the student in control of meaning-making.
